svg.title: Two laws, two different questions
svg.desc: On the left, a schematic of a system drawn inside its surroundings, with the sign conventions used in chemistry. Heat flowing into the system is positive q and is endothermic; heat flowing out is negative q and is exothermic. Work done on the system, as in compression, is positive w; work done by the system, as in expansion against an external pressure, is negative w. Underneath, the convention warning: this course uses the chemistry convention, in which change in internal energy equals q plus w and both are positive when they add energy to the system, whereas many physics texts write change in internal energy equals q minus w with w meaning work done by the system; the two differ only in the sign attached to w. On the right, the two laws set side by side. The First Law: energy is conserved, change in internal energy equals q plus w, with pressure-volume work equal to minus external pressure times change in volume. At constant volume there is no work, so the change in internal energy equals the heat, which is what a bomb calorimeter measures. At constant pressure the heat equals the change in enthalpy, which is what the tables report. What the First Law cannot tell you is which direction a process will run, because energy is conserved whether coffee warms the room or the room warms the coffee. The Second Law: the entropy of the universe never decreases. The change in entropy of the universe equals the change for the system plus the change for the surroundings and is greater than or equal to zero, with equality only for a reversible process. The entropy of the surroundings equals minus the enthalpy change of the system divided by temperature at constant pressure, so a system's entropy may fall as long as the surroundings rise by at least as much. Boltzmann's relation, entropy equals Boltzmann's constant times the logarithm of the number of microstates, and the thermodynamic definition, change in entropy equals reversible heat over temperature, are both given. A footer strip gives the heuristics for the sign of an entropy change: more moles of gas on the product side increases entropy and fewer decreases it; solid to liquid to gas increases it, and the gas step is by far the largest; a gas expanding into a larger volume increases it; dissolving an ionic solid usually increases it, though strong hydration of small highly charged ions can reverse that; polymerising many monomers into one chain decreases it; and raising the temperature increases it. A final note distinguishes state functions, internal energy, enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs free energy, which depend only on the current state, from the path functions heat and work, whose values depend on how the change was made.
svg.text: Two laws, two different questions
The First Law asks how much. The Second asks which way. You need both, and they answer nothing of each other's business.
SURROUNDINGS
SYSTEM
what you are actually
calculating
q > 0 in
q < 0 out
w > 0 on
w < 0 by
ΔU = q + w
Which convention?
This course uses the chemistry convention above: ΔU = q
+ w, and both are positive when they add energy to the
system. Many physics texts write ΔU = q − w, where w
means work done *by* the system. Same physics; opposite
sign on w. Check before you substitute.
FIRST LAW — how much?
Energy is conserved. ΔU = q + w, with PV work w = −PₑₓₜΔV.
Constant volume: w = 0, so ΔU = qᵥ — what a bomb calorimeter measures.
Constant pressure: qₚ = ΔH — what the tables report.
For gases: ΔH = ΔU + Δn_gas·RT.
What it cannot tell you: which way. Energy is conserved whether the coffee
warms the room or the room warms the coffee.
SECOND LAW — which way?
The entropy of the universe never decreases.
ΔS_univ = ΔS_sys + ΔS_surr ≥ 0, with equality only for a reversible
process.
ΔS_surr = −ΔH_sys / T (constant pressure).
S = k_B·ln W · ΔS = q_rev / T.
So a system's entropy may fall — water freezing, a protein folding —
provided the surroundings rise by at least as much.
Predicting the sign of ΔS without calculating anything
More moles of gas on the right → ΔS > 0 (fewer → ΔS < 0) · solid → liquid → gas, the gas step far the largest · gas expanding into a
larger volume · dissolving an ionic solid, usually (strong hydration of small, highly charged ions can reverse it) · many monomers →
one polymer → ΔS < 0 · raising T → ΔS > 0.
State functions versus path functions
U, H, S and G depend only on where the system is now, so Δ is final minus initial whatever route was taken — which is why Hess's Law
works, and why you may compute ΔS for an irreversible change along any convenient reversible path. q and w are path functions: their
values depend on how you got there.
